CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold our current posture and pursue a negotiated path at the scheduled G20 meeting in Buenos Aires rather than escalating further. We should keep retaliation measured and proportional if provoked, but use the imminent Xi-Trump summit and the warm Nov 1 phone call as the opening to seek a framework deal on purchases (agricultural/energy) while firmly defending our positions on IP and industrial policy. Do not escalate pre-emptively: an escalation now invites the threatened additional $267B of tariffs and the scheduled Jan 1, 2019 rise of the $200B List-3 tariff to 25%, exactly when our growth is already decelerating.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat to China is high and rising. US Section 301 tariffs already cover roughly $250B of our exports (List 1 $34B at 25% on Jul 6; List 2 $16B on Aug 23; List 3 $200B at 10% on Sep 24) with the $200B tranche set to jump to 25% on Jan 1 and a further $267B threatened — essentially all China-US trade (event_timeline). The real economy is already showing the strain: Q3 GDP slowed to 6.5%, the weakest since 2009, October official manufacturing PMI fell to 50.2 (lowest since July 2016), and new export orders contracted for a fifth straight month to 46.9, with SME sub-indices in contraction and the yuan under depreciation pressure (Reuters, CNBC, Politico, Oct 31). Firm-level targeting is the live non-tariff threat — the ZTE denial order in April and the looming Huawei risk directly pressure our export champions and Made-in-China-2025 tech-autonomy goals. A 25% tariff on all trade could shave ~1.2pp off 2019 GDP per Moody's (politico.com, Oct 31). This is a material, high-level threat — above the +0.5 'high' anchor — though not yet existential: exports have held up on front-loading, we hold deep FX reserves and policy room (RRR cuts, export rebates, stimulus), and the G20 channel is open. That justifies action_score leaning toward de-escalation (negotiate, +0.1) rather than escalation: a hawkish move would crystallize the Jan 1 25% hike and the $267B threat at the moment our export order book is weakest, whereas the Nov 1 Xi-Trump call — described as 'long and very good,' with Xi eager to lower the temperature and Trump signaling openness to scaling back tariffs if talks succeed (NYT, USA Today, Nov 1-2) — gives us a realistic off-ramp. We should not unilaterally concede structural reform or purchasing commitments before a matching US offer, so negotiate/hold-current-stance is the right level, not full concession.
key_factors: US Section 301 tariffs on ~$250B of Chinese exports, with $200B at 10% scheduled to rise to 25% on Jan 1, 2019
Threatened additional $267B tariffs = virtually all China-US trade
Q3 2018 GDP growth 6.5% — slowest since 2009; Oct PMI 50.2, lowest since 2016; new export orders contracted 5th straight month
Non-tariff tech targeting: ZTE denial order precedent, looming Huawei entity-list / supply-chain risk
Yuan depreciation pressure against a broadly stronger dollar
G20 Buenos Aires meeting scheduled, following a warm, 56-minute Xi-Trump phone call on Nov 1
China retains policy room (RRR cuts, export rebates, stimulus) and deep reserves to cushion the shock

Trump and Xi hold a phone call focused on trade; agree to meet at the G20 in Argentina.
Official PMI fell to 50.2 in October, lowest since July 2016... new export orders contracted for a fifth straight month to 46.9.
Moody's estimated that a 25% tariff on all China-US trade... China's GDP growth would fall by 1.2 percentage points to 5.2% in 2019.
Xi issued a similarly warm statement... predicting the two sides could reach a deal. Chinese officials... eager to lower the temperature.
Third-quarter GDP grew by 6.5% from a year ago - the weakest result since Q1 2009... authorities have eased bank financing costs, taxes and increased export rebates for the second time this year.
